Comment 1.1: In this paper, the confidence head is treated as a per-pixel uncertainty estimator. However, its output is produced by a small CNN trained jointly with the correction modules, and no explicit loss function is provided to enforce its interpretation as confidence or uncertainty. Therefore, it remains unclear why this learned map should be regarded as a calibrated confidence estimate rather than simply another latent attention or gating map.
Comment 1.2: The six predicate maps P1 to P6 are central to the proposed neuro-symbolic correction framework. However, the current ablation study does not sufficiently validate their necessity or individual contributions. The authors should provide predicate-level ablation experiments, such as leave-one-predicate-out settings for P1 to P6, to show whether each predicate contributes to the corresponding image-quality improvement.
Comment 1.3: The correction modules may improve image-quality metrics by enhancing contrast and edges. However, they may also introduce artificial sharpening or alter subtle anatomical structures. The manuscript should discuss this potential risk more explicitly, especially regarding whether the proposed correction could hallucinate boundaries, suppress weak structures, or modify clinically relevant details.
Comment 1.4: The design of the fuzzy rules and their coefficients requires further discussion. Although the use of Lukasiewicz fuzzy logic is mathematically well-defined, the particular combinations of predicates and manually selected weights, such as 1.5 and 2.0, appear heuristic. The authors should discuss the rationale behind these choices and provide sensitivity or ablation studies with alternative rule structures and weight settings.
Comment 1.5: The literature review on the Deep expert network with neuro-symbolic AI is insufficient. The authors should expand the Introduction and Discussion to include those recent works.
Comment 1.6: Although this work is well written, there are still some typo and grammar errors in the manuscript. Please check the manuscript and revise them.
Comment 2.1: Please clarify the exact cross-dataset and leave-one-out training protocol for Duke17 and Duke2013. The manuscript states that the corrector is trained once on PKU37 and transferred to the external datasets, but the experimental section also describes LOO evaluation as training on n-1 images and testing on the held-out image. It should be explicitly stated which components, if any, are trained, fine-tuned, calibrated, or threshold-adjusted using the n-1 Duke samples in each fold.
Comment 2.2: Please add a short practical discussion of the observed PSNR decrease, particularly the relatively larger reduction for SwinIR on PKU37, and explain when the improvement in clinical metrics would justify this fidelity trade-off in real OCT applications.
Comment 3.1: You should better highlight the new ideas of this paper.
Comment 3.2: The motivation of your approach requires better highlighting as well.
Comment 3.3: Besides, the following ideas on modeling are recommended to be included because of their successful applications in various fields. Evolving fuzzy models of shape memory alloy wire actuators (RJIST 2021), Model-data-driven image reconstruction with neural networks for ultrasound computed tomography breast imaging (NEUCOM 2022), Effect of random variation of the initial values of ordinary differential equations and its web-based application to chemical kinetics (RJIST 2025).
Comment 3.4: How do you define the stability?
Comment 3.5: Optimization is mentioned within the paper. Which is the optimization problem and how is it solved? Optimization could be well linked to learning.
Comment 3.6: You are using embedded notations, which are understood by a narrow area of readers.
Comment 3.7: You should define the operator used in (6).
Comment 3.8: Is the operator dot the classical algebraic multiplication? If yes, you could drop it out.
Comment 3.9: The six ground-truth-free predicates should be justified clinically and mathematically. The authors should provide sensitivity analyses showing how each predicate and its spatial failure map influence the final correction.
Comment 3.10: The training algorithm is not sufficiently clear. Please describe the training targets, loss functions, initialization, parameter selection, and whether any clean or paired images are used indirectly.
Comment 3.11: Since post correction can introduce artificial boundaries or suppress subtle pathological features, stronger safety validation is essential. Experiments should examine lesions, fluid regions, thin layers, and other clinically relevant structures, preferably with expert assessment.
Comment 3.12: A better link of the theory treated in the initial sections to the application given in Section VI is needed.
Comment 3.13: In this regard, you should save the programs and datasets of Section VI in a webpage or repository, and indicate a link to that webpage, without any password, to be used only during the review process.
Comment 3.14: Solving the comment 13 will enable the improvement of the validation.
Comment 3.15: You should not use experiment and experimental in title of Section VI, the other section titles and the rest of the paper. You are not doing experiments, you are actually doing tests on three retinal OCT datasets. You could use test or results instead.
Comment 3.16: A fair comparison means to work with competing models with a similar complexity and designed using the same design approach.
Comment 3.17: How did you compute the parameters of the fuzzy logic part of the paper? Certain heuristics might be therein.
Comment 3.18: The transferability claim requires further evidence. Adapting a backbone-specific confidence head constitutes additional training, therefore the required data, computational cost, and performance variability for each backbone should be reported.
Comment 3.19: The authors could verify whether the assumed Lipschitz constants, margins, and background-leakage bounds hold for the experimental data.
